_slice: Alberta provincial social and benefit programs
_note: Alberta's income-tested social programmes turn out to have a much tidier shape than expected, because in 2025-26 the province collapsed almost all of its benefit indexation onto a single parameter. From 2023 to 2025, AISH, Income Support and the Alberta Seniors Benefit were each separately indexed to the Alberta all-items CPI published by Statistics Canada, with an explicit October-to-September averaging formula written into each policy manual. Bill 32 (Financial Statutes Amendment Act, 2024) replaced that with the 'Alberta escalator' defined in s. 44.2 of the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act - the lesser of 2% and the same Alberta CPI change - and then had the AISH Act, the Income and Employment Supports Act and the Seniors Benefit Act all point at that one definition. The result is a hub-and-spoke pattern: statcan-cpi feeds the Alberta escalator, which feeds AISH/ADAP rates, Income Support core essential and core shelter rates, the Alberta Child and Family Benefit parameters, and the Alberta Seniors Benefit cash benefit, with the 2% cap biting in both 2025 and 2026. Two things sit outside that hub and are the more interesting findings. First, accommodation charges are deliberately carved out of every benefit's escalator and pinned instead to the maximum charge set under the Continuing Care Act, so the AISH modified living allowance, Income Support for continuing care residents, and the Seniors Benefit Supplementary Accommodation Benefit all depend on an Alberta Health price table. Second, the Seniors Benefit Act escalates its non-deductible income amount by the federal Canada Pension Plan Pension Index, not the Alberta escalator, and writes federal OAS and GIS maximums directly into its benefit formulas. Health-side programmes (Alberta Adult Health Benefit, Alberta Aids to Daily Living) are the opposite case: their income thresholds carry no documented indexation rule at all, and the AAHB table has not moved since 2015 - those non-edges are recorded in _dropped. This slice runs slightly above the suggested edge count because the escalator reform gave several programmes two separately documented indexation edges (the pre-2026 direct CPI rule and the post-2026 escalator rule); both are kept because both are stated in the source documents.

reports.title: AISH/ADAP Financial Benefits Summary (benefit rate schedule)
reports.publisher: Alberta Assisted Living and Social Services
reports.description: The annual schedule of dollar amounts paid under Assured Income for the Severely Handicapped (AISH) and, from July 2026, the Alberta Disability Assistance Program (ADAP). It sets the monthly living allowance, modified living allowance personal allowance, child benefit, personal benefit maximums and the employment and passive-income exemption thresholds. Rates are revised effective January 1 each year and republished as a fact sheet alongside the Disability Income Assistance Policy Manual.
reports.cadence_note: Rates take effect January 1; the summary fact sheet is revised at that date (the 2026 edition is marked 'Rev. 2026-01'). Off-cycle republication occurs when the programme itself changes, as with the July 2, 2026 AISH/ADAP split.

release_schedule.rule: AISH (and now ADAP) benefit rates are indexed annually to the Alberta Consumer Price Index (CPI), effective January 1 of each year, based on the prior year's Alberta CPI change. Indexing was introduced under Bill 26 starting January 2019, paused 2020-2022, and restored beginning January 2023 under the Inflation Relief Act; the January 1, 2026 adjustment raised the maximum AISH living allowance from $1,901 to $1,940/month.

entries.covers: Annual Alberta CPI-indexed adjustment to AISH/ADAP benefit rate schedule

release_schedule.note: No dated release calendar exists; the publisher's own AISH 'Indexing of Benefits' page (humanservices.alberta.ca/AWOnline/AISH/8629.html) states the rule but blocks automated fetch via robots.txt. Corroborated via secondary sources (lifemoney.ca, Wikipedia AISH article) citing the January 2026 rate ($1,940) as the result of the annual January 1 CPI indexation restored in 2023. Next occurrence computed as Jan 1, 2027 since Jan 1, 2026 has already passed.

reports.title: Alberta Escalator (Alberta Personal Income Tax Act indexation factor)
reports.description: The annual indexation factor defined in section 44.2 of the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act and published each year by Treasury Board and Finance alongside the personal income tax bracket table. For years after 2025 it is either a percentage prescribed by regulation before January 1, or, absent a prescription, the lesser of 2% and the year-over-year change in the Alberta Consumer Price Index over the 12 months ending September 30. It is the single escalator that now drives Alberta tax brackets and credit amounts, the Alberta Child and Family Benefit, and AISH/ADAP benefit rates.
reports.cadence_note: One factor per taxation year, effective January 1; published in the personal income tax bracket table and in the Budget tax plan.

release_schedule.rule: If no percentage is prescribed by regulation by January 1, a CPI-derived formula (capped at 2%) applies automatically.
release_schedule.note: A 2026 amendment to this section exists but is not yet in force as of this audit — worth rechecking before relying on this rule going forward.

reports.title: Alberta Child and Family Benefit (ACFB) maximum benefit amounts and thresholds
reports.publisher: Alberta Treasury Board and Finance (delivered by the Canada Revenue Agency)
reports.description: The schedule of base component and working component maximum amounts, the working-income entry threshold, and the family net income phase-out thresholds for the Alberta Child and Family Benefit. The dollar amounts sit in section 30.2(2) of the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act and are restated each year on alberta.ca. The benefit year runs July to June and payments are issued quarterly by the CRA on Alberta's behalf.
reports.cadence_note: Amounts are set for a July-to-June benefit year and adjusted once a year; the CRA pays them out in four quarterly instalments (August, November, February, May).

entries.covers: ACFB maximum amounts and thresholds for benefit year July 2025-June 2026
ACFB maximum amounts and thresholds for benefit year July 2026-June 2027
ACFB maximum amounts and thresholds for benefit year July 2027-June 2028 (projected)

release_schedule.note: The alberta.ca ACFB page currently publishes maximum benefit amounts and income thresholds for two consecutive 'benefit years' (July 2025-June 2026 and July 2026-June 2027), with different dollar figures for each, showing the figures are updated annually to coincide with the start of each new benefit year on July 1. No explicit indexation statute or fixed publication calendar was found on the page itself, so this is inferred from the observed year-over-year pattern rather than a stated rule. Payment dates (the quarterly disbursement schedule of Aug/Nov/Feb/May) are a separate, unrelated cadence from the annual update of maximum amounts/thresholds, which is what this corpus entry tracks.

reports.title: Alberta Seniors Benefit maximum benefit amounts, income thresholds and phase-out rates
reports.publisher: Alberta Assisted Living and Social Services (Seniors Financial Assistance)
reports.description: The annual schedule of maximum Alberta Seniors Benefit amounts by accommodation category and marital status, the income guideline thresholds, and the phase-out rates applied per dollar of non-deductible income. It also governs the Supplementary Accommodation Benefit for seniors in continuing care homes. Amounts take effect at the start of each July-to-June benefit year and are calculated from the applicant's previous calendar year income as reported to the Canada Revenue Agency.
reports.cadence_note: Benefit year runs July 1 to June 30 (the current schedule is stated as 'Effective July 1, 2026'); benefits are paid monthly.

release_schedule.note: No published forward calendar and no statute text specifying exact review dates was found on alberta.ca; the schedule is inferred from the Open Government dataset's release history, which shows new editions of the 'Alberta Seniors Benefit thresholds rates and percentages' document released consistently around January 1 and July 1 each year since at least 2023 (and July-only in 2020-2022, January-only in 2019). The alberta.ca program page confirms current thresholds are stated 'as of July 1, 2026'. The July 2026 edition (created 2026-07-09 on open.alberta.ca) is the current/active one as of the 2026-08-11 research date, so the next expected editions are January 2027 and July 2027. Occasional additional interim updates have also occurred (e.g. April 2024, April 2026), so mid-cycle revisions are possible.

reports.title: Alberta Income Support core benefit rate schedule (core essential and core shelter)
reports.publisher: Alberta Assisted Living and Social Services
reports.description: The schedule of Income Support core essential payments (including the comforts allowance) and core shelter payments by household composition, set under the Income and Employment Supports Act and the Income Support, Training and Health Benefits Regulation, together with the supplementary benefit maximums. Rates apply to both the Expected to Work (ETW) and Barriers to Full Employment (BFE) client streams and are revised effective January 1 each year through the 'Benefit Rate Adjustments' policy in the Income and Employment Supports Policy Manual.
reports.cadence_note: Rate adjustment takes effect January 1 each year; the manual's Core Shelter Rate Adjustment and Core Essential Rate Adjustment pages carry the year-specific tables.

entries.covers: Annual indexation of Core Essential and Core Shelter benefit rates

release_schedule.rule: Core Essential and Core Shelter benefit amounts are indexed annually, effective January 1 each year, to the Alberta Consumer Price Index (with increases capped at a maximum of 2 per cent under Alberta's indexation legislation, the "Alberta Escalator"). Note: Core Shelter-Social Housing rate increases instead take effect at each recipient's individual Annual Rent Review rather than on January 1.
release_schedule.note: Alberta resumed CPI indexing of income supports effective Jan 1, 2023; most recently confirmed indexation events occurred Jan 1, 2024 (4.25%) and Jan 1, 2026 (2%, per Maytree). New provincial legislation caps annual indexation at a maximum of 2%. The base URL alberta.ca/income-support itself has no calendar or rate table; rate figures and the indexing rule are documented on secondary/advocacy sites citing Alberta government sources (Maytree, enoughforall.ca) rather than a single official calendar page.

reports.title: Continuing Care Resident Accommodation Charges (maximum charges, types A and B)
reports.description: The table of maximum daily resident accommodation charges that type A and type B continuing care homes may charge, set by the Alberta government under the Continuing Care (Ministerial) Regulation. It also fixes the Alternate Level of Care charge for hospital patients awaiting a continuing care space. These charges are the accommodation component of the AISH/ADAP modified living allowance and of Income Support benefits for clients in continuing care, and they set the ceiling for the Alberta Seniors Benefit Supplementary Accommodation Benefit.
reports.cadence_note: Adjusted annually for inflation; the 2026 adjustment took effect August 1, 2026 (a 1.8% increase) rather than on the previous April 1 cycle, so the effective date has moved between years.

release_schedule.rule: Effective August 1 [each year], the maximum accommodation charges will increase ... to reflect the annual inflation adjustment.

entries.covers: Annual inflation adjustment to maximum resident accommodation charges (Type A and B)

release_schedule.note: Alberta.ca states the current August 1, 2026 adjustment already took effect (1.8% increase, 'annual inflation adjustment'), confirmed by Alberta Continuing Care Association news post stating 'the annual adjustment to the maximum accommodation charges will take effect August 1, 2026.' Since today (2026-08-11) is after that date, the next occurrence is projected to August 1, 2027 following the same annual pattern. A separate April 1, 2026 effective date is also shown on the page for the 'current' rate table, but the recurring adjustment cycle publisher describes as annual is the August 1 inflation adjustment.

reports.title: Health Benefits: Qualifying Income Levels Ministerial Order (Alberta Adult Health Benefit and Alberta Child Health Benefit)
reports.publisher: Alberta Assisted Living and Social Services
reports.description: The Ministerial Order made under the Income and Employment Supports Act that sets the maximum qualifying income levels by household type for the Alberta Adult Health Benefit (dental, optical, prescription drug, ambulance and diabetic supply coverage) and the Alberta Child Health Benefit. Financial eligibility at application and at annual renewal is tested against total combined household net income plus non-taxable child support. The order is reproduced in the Income and Employment Supports Policy Manual.
reports.cadence_note: Amended by Ministerial Order rather than on a fixed calendar. The qualifying income level table in the policy manual is still dated July 1, 2015, so in most years the order is re-affirmed rather than re-issued; the AAHB benefit period itself runs October 1 to September 30 with an automated annual renewal.

release_schedule.rule: Income Support, Training and Health Benefits Regulation (Alta Reg 122/2011), ss. 87-90: a household is financially eligible for the Alberta Adult Health Benefit / Alberta Child Health Benefit if its assessed income is equal to or less than 'the qualifying income level as determined by the Minister.' The Regulation does not specify any fixed interval at which the Minister must set or revise that level.
release_schedule.note: This is not a recurring statistical publication but a discretionary ministerial determination embedded in regulation (most recently amended by AR 97/2026, current-as-of-July-2026 consolidation). No dated release calendar or fixed-interval rule for updating the dollar qualifying-income-level table was found on alberta.ca, the King's Printer regulation text, or open.alberta.ca. The alberta.ca program page and a 2009 predecessor fact sheet both state that individual recipients' financial eligibility is 'reviewed annually' / confirmed 'every September' against CRA income data - but that describes re-verifying an existing recipient's continued eligibility against the current threshold, not a commitment to reissue or change the threshold table itself on that date. Alberta Ombudsman's 2024 investigation into AAHB/ACHB flagged systemic problems including thresholds that had gone without update for extended periods, which is more consistent with ad hoc/irregular ministerial revisions than a fixed annual release. Given this, releases_per_year=1 in the corpus is not well supported by direct evidence; if anything the evidence points to this being an irregular, discretion-driven instrument rather than a fixed-cadence release, though I could not find a citation strong enough to assert a specific correct replacement number.

reports.title: Alberta Aids to Daily Living cost-share amounts and cost-share exemption income thresholds
reports.publisher: Alberta Health (Alberta Aids to Daily Living)
reports.description: The published cost-share rules for the Alberta Aids to Daily Living programme: clients pay 25% of the cost of most benefits up to a maximum of $500 per family per benefit year, and the taxable-income thresholds below which a client is exempt. It also lists the provincial income programmes whose recipients may be exempt from cost-sharing. The benefit year runs July 1 to June 30.
reports.cadence_note: Cost-share maximum and exemption thresholds are stated per benefit year (July 1 to June 30) and revised when Alberta Health changes them; the 25%/$500 structure has been stable for years while the exemption thresholds move.

release_schedule.note: The alberta.ca cost-sharing page presents the 25%/$500 maximum cost-share and income exemption thresholds as static figures with no stated review cycle, effective date, or calendar. The most closely related governing document (AADL Program Manual Section GN - general policy and procedures) has been revised at irregular intervals (Sep 2024, Sep 2023, Jan 2023, Jul 2022, Feb 2021, Dec 2020, Feb 2020, Sep 2017, Jan 2017...) rather than on a fixed annual schedule, and no source states a rule (e.g. 'reviewed every X months') governing when cost-share amounts/income thresholds themselves change. No evidence of a published calendar or a consistent annual pattern specific to this parameter was found.

dependencies.basis: The archived 2023-2025 version of the 'Indexing of Benefits' policy in the Alberta AISH policy manual (retained on the current Benefit Rate Adjustments page) states: 'AISH benefits are adjusted annually using the Alberta Consumer Price Index (CPI) starting on January 1, 2023 ... Annual benefit rate changes are calculated using the Alberta CPI (All-items, not seasonally adjusted). The Alberta CPI is published monthly by Statistics Canada and measures the change in price for goods and services bought by Albertans.' It sets out the formula X = A/B - 1, where A is the sum of the monthly Alberta CPI indexes for the 12 months ending September 30 before the adjustment date and B is the sum for the preceding 12 months. From January 1, 2026 the dependence on Alberta CPI is mediated by the Alberta escalator, which is capped at 2%.

reference_period.stated_as: 'A is the sum of the monthly Alberta CPI indexes for the 12 months ending September 30 before the adjustment date'.

dependencies.evidence_quote: How Benefits are Adjusted Annual benefit rate changes are calculated using the standard escalator amount established in the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act, which is the lesser of either two per cent, or the Alberta Consumer Price Index (CPI) amount from October through September year-over-year.

dependencies.basis: The current 'Benefit Rate Adjustments' policy (last updated July 2, 2026) in the Disability Income Assistance Policy Manual states: 'AISH and ADAP benefit rates are adjusted annually, effective January 1st of each year. Starting January 1, 2026, the rate of adjustment is based on the standard escalator amount established under section 44.2 of the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act.' It adds: 'Annual benefit rate changes are calculated using the standard escalator amount established in the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act, which is the lesser of either two per cent, or the Alberta Consumer Price Index (CPI) amount from October through September year-over-year.' The policy cites as authority the AISH Act s. 3.1(2), the AISH General Regulations s. 7(3) and the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act s. 44.2. Living allowance, the modified living allowance personal allowance, the child benefit and most personal benefits are adjusted; health benefits and actual-cost benefits are not.

reference_period.stated_as: 'AISH and ADAP benefit rates are adjusted annually, effective January 1st of each year', on the s.44.2 escalator.

dependencies.evidence_quote: AISH and ADAP benefit rates are adjusted annually, effective January 1st of each year. Starting January 1, 2026, the rate of adjustment is based on the standard escalator amount established under section 44.2 of the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act.

dependencies.basis: Alberta Personal Income Tax Act, RSA 2000 c A-30, s. 44.2(0.1)(b) defines the Alberta escalator, absent a prescribed percentage, as the lesser of 2% and the amount determined by the formula A/B - 1, 'where A is the Consumer Price Index for Alberta for the 12-month period that ended on the last September 30 before that year, and B is the Consumer Price Index for Alberta for the 12-month period immediately preceding'. Subsection 44.2(3) then defines that index explicitly: 'the Consumer Price Index for Alberta for any 12-month period is the result arrived at by (a) aggregating the Consumer Price Index for Alberta, as published by Statistics Canada under the authority of the Statistics Act (Canada) ... for each month in that period, (b) dividing the aggregate ... by 12'.

reference_period.stated_as: 'A is the Consumer Price Index for Alberta for the 12-month period that ended on the last September 30 before that year' — Alberta Personal Income Tax Act s.44.2(0.1)(b).

dependencies.evidence_quote: the Consumer Price Index for Alberta for any 12-month period is the result arrived at by (a) aggregating the Consumer Price Index for Alberta, as published by Statistics Canada under the authority of the Statistics Act (Canada) ... for each month in that period, (b) dividing the aggregate ... by 12

dependencies.basis: Alberta Personal Income Tax Act, RSA 2000 c A-30, s. 44.2(2): 'Where the base taxation year ... in relation to a particular month is after 2024, each of the amounts expressed in dollars in section 30.2(2), except the amount of $2760, is to be adjusted so that the amount to be used under that subsection for the month is the total of (a) the amount that would, but for subsection (4), be the amount used under section 30.2(2) for the month that is one year before the particular month, and (b) the product obtained by multiplying (i) the amount referred to in clause (a) by (ii) the Alberta escalator for the taxation year following the base taxation year.' Section 30.2(2) is the Alberta Child and Family Benefit formula, containing the per-child base and working component amounts and the net income phase-out thresholds. The $2,760 working-income entry threshold is expressly excluded from indexation.

The Seniors Benefit Act (RSA 2000 c S-7) Schedule puts federal OAS and GIS amounts directly inside the Alberta formulas. Schedule s. 9(2)(b)(ii) sets the special needs component income test as 'the sum of (A) the single senior non-deductible income amount under section 8 for the benefit adjustment year, plus (B) an amount equal to the maximum annual amount, not including retroactive payments and not adjusted for deferral, of the monthly pension payable to a single senior under the Old Age Security Act (Canada) in the calendar year that ended before the commencement of the benefit adjustment year.' Schedule s. 7(4) defines term C of the supplementary accommodation assistance formula as 'the combined maximum annual amount ... of Old Age Security, not adjusted for deferral, and Guaranteed Income Supplement payable to a single senior and the maximum benefit payable to a single senior under section 4, in the previous calendar year.' The programme page corroborates that receipt of OAS is an eligibility condition and that lines 11300 (OAS) and 14600 (net federal supplements: GIS and Allowance) are deducted in arriving at non-deductible income (https://www.alberta.ca/alberta-seniors-benefit).
dependencies.evidence_quote: the sum of (A) the single senior non-deductible income amount under section 8 for the benefit adjustment year, plus (B) an amount equal to the maximum annual amount, not including retroactive payments and not adjusted for deferral, of the monthly pension payable to a single senior under the Old Age Security Act (Canada) in the calendar year that ended before the commencement of the benefit adjustment year.

dependencies.basis: Seniors Benefit Act, RSA 2000 c S-7, s. 1(a.21): "'Alberta escalator' means the Alberta escalator as defined in section 44.2 of the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act". The Schedule, s. 2 ('Calculation of adjusted benefit amounts'), then provides: 'A benefit or an amount used to calculate a benefit or eligibility for a benefit that is to be adjusted under section 2.1(3)(b), (3.1)(b) or (5)(a)(ii) or 2.2(3)(b) or (5)(b) of this Act must be adjusted by an amount equal to (a) the benefit amount or amount as of December 31 of the previous calendar year, including any increase to that amount made under this Act or the regulations, multiplied by (b) the Alberta escalator.' So the Alberta Seniors Benefit annual cash benefit and the amounts used to calculate eligibility for it move with the same 2%-capped escalator as AISH, Income Support and the ACFB.

Seniors Benefit Act Schedule, s. 8: '(1) The non-deductible income amount is (a) $23 020 for single seniors, and (b) $34 460 for senior couples. (2) Effective the benefit adjustment date of each benefit adjustment year, the non-deductible income amount is the non-deductible income amount in the previous benefit adjustment year increased annually by a percentage equivalent to the Pension Index under the Canada Pension Plan (Canada) that was applicable for the calendar year that ended before the commencement of the benefit adjustment year.' Subsection (3) adds a fallback: the Minister, in consultation with the Minister responsible for the Financial Administration Act, determines the adjustment 'if (a) the method of calculating the Pension Index is modified by the Government of Canada, or (b) the change in the Pension Index cannot be determined for any reason.' This is a rare case of an Alberta benefit threshold being escalated by a federal index rather than the Alberta escalator.
dependencies.evidence_quote: (1) The non-deductible income amount is (a) $23 020 for single seniors, and (b) $34 460 for senior couples. (2) Effective the benefit adjustment date of each benefit adjustment year, the non-deductible income amount is the non-deductible income amount in the previous benefit adjustment year increased annually by a percentage equivalent to the Pension Index under the Canada Pension Plan (Canada) that was applicable for the calendar year that ended before the commencement of the benefit adjustment year.

dependencies.basis: The 'Benefit Rate Adjustments' policy in the Income and Employment Supports Policy Manual cites as authority the Income and Employment Supports Act s. 1(a.01), the Income Support, Training and Health Benefits Regulation s. 24.2, and the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act s. 44.2, and states: 'Income Support benefit rates are adjusted annually, effective January 1st of each year. Starting January 1, 2026, the rate of adjustment is based on the standard escalator amount established under section 44.2 of the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act.' It specifies that the adjusted core benefits are 'Core essential payment including the comforts allowance' and 'Core shelter payment', and that supplementary benefits are adjusted except where they are actual-cost, set by agreement, or set in separate legislation.

Annual benefit rate changes are calculated using the Alberta CPI (All-items, not seasonally adjusted). The Alberta CPI is published monthly by Statistics Canada'. The AISH Financial Benefits Summary makes the same point about the modified living allowance: 'The accommodation room rate charges are established under the Continuing Care Act.' The accommodation component of an Income Support client's benefit therefore tracks the Alberta Health maximum accommodation charge table rather than the Alberta escalator.

A is the maximum monthly accommodation charge set under the Continuing Care Act in respect of a private room that is in effect on the first day of the month after the accommodation adjustment date; B is the monthly disposable income amount added to the maximum monthly accommodation charge under subsection (2)(a)'. The programme page restates this in plain language - the Supplementary Accommodation Benefit is determined by 'the maximum monthly accommodation charge for a private room in a continuing care home' and 'the monthly disposable income amount of at least $373' - and the Alberta Health charges page confirms it from the other side: 'accommodation charges may be fully or partly covered for low-income residents who are either eligible for the Alberta Seniors Benefit [or] clients of the Assured Income for the Severely Handicapped (AISH) program ... residents who are eligible for benefits through these programs will be assured of at least $373 per month in disposable income after their monthly accommodation charge is paid.'

dependencies.basis: The Disability Income Assistance Policy Manual 'Pension Income' policy (authority: AISH Act s. 3.2; AISH General Regulation s. 2.01(1)(c) and Schedule 1) lists 'CPP Disability' among the pension income sources and states: 'Applicants and clients pension income is non-exempt and deducted dollar for dollar as this type of income is intended to cover basic living needs, similar to AISH and ADAP.' It also states the interaction at the margin: 'If clients' Canada Pension Plan - Disability benefits increase to the point where they are no longer eligible for the AISH or ADAP monthly living allowance, they will continue to receive the same health coverage they had on AISH or ADAP through the Alberta Adult Health Benefit (AAHB) program.' The CPP-D amount is therefore a direct, dollar-for-dollar input to the AISH/ADAP payment calculation.

The same 'Pension Income' policy lists 'Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS)', 'Old Age Security', 'Old Age Security Allowance (spouse)' and 'Old Age Security Supplement (survivor)' as pension income, and then makes federal OAS/GIS receipt a hard eligibility bar: 'Applicants and clients receiving the following pension income(s) are not eligible to receive AISH or ADAP: Alberta Seniors Benefits (except for where the applicant or client is 65 years old or older and they have not lived in Canada long enough to receive Old Age Security); Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS); or Old Age Security.' Where it is not disqualifying, pension income is 'non-exempt and deducted dollar for dollar'.

dependencies.evidence_quote: The Alberta Adult Health Benefit (AAHB) program provides health benefits to clients who no longer qualify for AISH or ADAP due to income from: Employment or self-employment income of a cohabiting partner; The Canada Pension Plan Disability (CPP-D) program; or a combination of these and other types of income that are not exempt through AISH or ADAP.

dependencies.basis: The AAHB policy in the Disability Income Assistance Policy Manual states its purpose as 'To assist eligible former AISH and ADAP clients to maintain health benefits when they no longer qualify for AISH or ADAP', and describes the handover mechanically: 'When an AISH or ADAP client enrols in the AAHB program, health coverage transitions from AISH or ADAP to the AAHB program without interruption.' Entry to AAHB is triggered by the AISH/ADAP income test - that is, by the AISH exemption thresholds and living allowance in the AISH benefit rate schedule - and clients can return to AISH or ADAP from AAHB without a new application in most circumstances.
dependencies.evidence_quote: To assist eligible former AISH and ADAP clients to maintain health benefits when they no longer qualify for AISH or ADAP

dependencies.basis: The AADL cost-sharing page states that 'client[s] pay 25% of the cost of program benefits up to a maximum of $500 per family per benefit year (July 1 to June 30)' and that 'Clients receiving income supplement benefits from the following Alberta government programs may be exempt from cost-sharing: Income Support Program benefits; Assured Income for the Severely Handicapped (AISH); Alberta Adult Health Benefits (AAHB); Child and Youth Support Program; Children and Family Services (minors in foster care).' Enrolment in AISH (or Income Support, or AAHB) is therefore a direct input to whether a client owes the AADL cost-share; the page also instructs clients to contact AADL if they receive AISH or Alberta Works health benefits. The alternative test is a taxable income threshold on line 26000 of the most recent income tax return.
dependencies.evidence_quote: Clients receiving income supplement benefits from the following Alberta government programs may be exempt from cost-sharing: Income Support Program benefits; Assured Income for the Severely Handicapped (AISH); Alberta Adult Health Benefits (AAHB); Child and Youth Support Program; Children and Family Services (minors in foster care).

dependencies.basis: The 2026-29 Fiscal Plan (Budget 2026) is where the new disability assistance rate structure is set out: 'On July 1, 2026, the new Alberta Disability Assistance Program (ADAP) will start ... The maximum ADAP benefit rate will be set at $1,740 per month. Clients who transition from AISH to ADAP will receive a transition benefit of $200 per month, maintaining the maximum total benefit at the same level as AISH until December 31, 2027. As with AISH, ADAP benefit rates will be subject to the Alberta escalator policy annually, and former ADAP clients will continue to receive ongoing health benefits until age 65, regardless of employment income.' The Budget therefore sets the starting level that the escalator subsequently indexes.

dependencies.basis: The 2026-29 Fiscal Plan sets the Alberta Seniors Benefit income thresholds directly: 'Effective July 1, 2026, the start of the 2026-27 benefit year, seniors' income thresholds for the Alberta Seniors Benefit will be reduced by 9 per cent, along with corresponding reductions for Special Needs Assistance for Seniors, and the grant component of the Seniors Home Adaptation and Repair Program thresholds, resulting in estimated savings of $23 million in 2026-27 and $31 million in 2027-28 and beyond.' A discretionary Budget decision can therefore override the statutory escalator in either direction for this programme.

The 2026-29 Fiscal Plan carries the 'Alberta Child and Family Benefit Program Parameters' table in its Tax Plan chapter, footnoted: 'Benefit amounts and phase-out thresholds have increased by 2% from 2025 due to the Alberta escalator.' The expense chapter explains the same movement in dollar terms: 'The Alberta Child and Family Benefit is budgeted at $405 million in 2026-27, an increase of $30 million, or 8 per cent from 2025-26 reflecting population growth, a 2 per cent escalator to benefit rates, and higher phase-out income thresholds.' The Budget is where the year's ACFB parameter table is authoritatively published.

dependencies.basis: RESOLVED 2026-08-09 (browser session, closing the item G.64.md left as cheap check 1). Continuing Care (Ministerial) Regulation, Alta Reg 44/2024 under the Continuing Care Act, SA 2022, c C-26.7 -- office consolidation with amendments up to and including AR 199/2025, current as of August 27, 2025, fetched in full via a Chrome browser session (a direct fetch-tool request to the same PDF URL returns ROBOTS_DISALLOWED; the King's Printer PDF itself carries no such restriction against ordinary browser access). Section 11 in full: '11(1) In this section, “Alberta CPI” means the monthly All-items Consumer Price Index for Alberta, not seasonally adjusted, published by Statistics Canada. (2) The maximum amount of the accommodation charge set by the Minister under section 9(4) of the Act in respect of each type of accommodation must be adjusted annually on August 1 by the lesser of the following: (a) the percentage increase in the Alberta CPI for the 12-month period ending on February 28 of that year, rounded to the nearest $0.05; (b) 3.8%.' This both settles the edge and explains the number on Alberta Health's programme page: the 1.8% increase stated to take effect August 1, 2026 is the CPI figure under (a), sitting below the 3.8% cap under (b) and so the binding term. Note the reference window is 12 months ending February 28, not September 30 as in the other Alberta-CPI edges in this slice -- this regulation runs its own, differently-dated formula.
